claim: Many metabolic enzymes self-assemble into micron-scale filaments to organize and regulate metabolism.
source: Many metabolic enzymes self-assemble into micron-scale filaments to organize and regulate metabolism.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by the broader literature context provided in the introduction.

claim: The appearance of metabolic enzyme assemblies often coincides with large metabolic changes as in development, cancer, and stress.
source: The appearance of these assemblies often coincides with large metabolic changes as in development, cancer, and stress.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about metabolic enzyme assemblies.

claim: Yeast undergo cytoplasmic acidification upon starvation.
source: Yeast undergo cytoplasmic acidification upon starvation, triggering the assembly of many metabolic enzymes into filaments.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript (Orij et al., 2009).

claim: Cytoplasmic acidification triggers the assembly of many metabolic enzymes into filaments in yeast.
source: Yeast undergo cytoplasmic acidification upon starvation, triggering the assembly of many metabolic enzymes into filaments.
evidence: This is supported by prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: CTPS assembles into metabolic filaments across many species.
source: CTP Synthase (CTPS) assembles into metabolic filaments across many species.
evidence: This is supported by citations throughout the manuscript (Carcamo et al., 2011; Ingerson-Mahar et al., 2010; Liu, 2010; Noree et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2021).

claim: Yeast CTPS filaments have a pH-sensitive assembly mechanism.
source: Cryo-EM structures reveal a pH-sensitive assembly mechanism and highly ordered filament bundles that stabilize an inactive state of the enzyme, features unique to yeast CTPS.
evidence: This is supported by structural data and biochemical assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Yeast CTPS filaments form highly ordered bundles.
source: Cryo-EM structures reveal a pH-sensitive assembly mechanism and highly ordered filament bundles that stabilize an inactive state of the enzyme, features unique to yeast CTPS.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 6.

claim: Yeast CTPS filament bundles stabilize an inactive state of the enzyme.
source: Cryo-EM structures reveal a pH-sensitive assembly mechanism and highly ordered filament bundles that stabilize an inactive state of the enzyme, features unique to yeast CTPS.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis showing closed ammonia channel and activity assays.

claim: The pH-sensitive assembly mechanism and highly ordered filament bundles are features unique to yeast CTPS.
source: Cryo-EM structures reveal a pH-sensitive assembly mechanism and highly ordered filament bundles that stabilize an inactive state of the enzyme, features unique to yeast CTPS.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with human and bacterial CTPS structures.

claim: Disruption of CTPS filaments in cells with non-assembly mutations decreases growth rate.
source: Disruption of filaments in cells with non-assembly or pH-insensitive mutations decreases growth rate, reflecting the importance of regulated CTPS filament assembly in homeotstasis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays with H360A and H360R mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: Disruption of CTPS filaments in cells with pH-insensitive mutations decreases growth rate.
source: Disruption of filaments in cells with non-assembly or pH-insensitive mutations decreases growth rate, reflecting the importance of regulated CTPS filament assembly in homeotstasis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays with H360R mutant shown in Figure 5.

claim: Regulated CTPS filament assembly is important for homeostasis.
source: Disruption of filaments in cells with non-assembly or pH-insensitive mutations decreases growth rate, reflecting the importance of regulated CTPS filament assembly in homeotstasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth defects observed in mutants.

claim: Metabolic enzyme self-assembly is a widespread mechanism of metabolic organization and regulation.
source: Only recently, however, have we come to appreciate the role of metabolic enzyme self-assembly as a widespread mechanism of metabolic organization and regulation (Lynch et al., 2020; Park and Horton, 2019; Simonet et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent reviews.

claim: Metabolic enzyme assemblies have been found in glycolysis.
source: These assemblies have been found in many core pathways including glycolysis (Kemp, 1971; Webb et al., 2017), fatty acid synthesis (Hunkeler et al., 2018; Kleinschmidt et al., 1969), amino acid synthesis (Cohen et al., 1976; Frey et al., 1975; Miller et al., 1974; Petrovska et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2018), and nucleotide synthesis (Barry et al., 2014; Carcamo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on glycolytic enzyme assemblies.

claim: Metabolic enzyme assemblies have been found in fatty acid synthesis.
source: These assemblies have been found in many core pathways including glycolysis (Kemp, 1971; Webb et al., 2017), fatty acid synthesis (Hunkeler et al., 2018; Kleinschmidt et al., 1969), amino acid synthesis (Cohen et al., 1976; Frey et al., 1975; Miller et al., 1974; Petrovska et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2018), and nucleotide synthesis (Barry et al., 2014; Carcamo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on fatty acid synthesis enzyme assemblies.

claim: Metabolic enzyme assemblies have been found in amino acid synthesis.
source: These assemblies have been found in many core pathways including glycolysis (Kemp, 1971; Webb et al., 2017), fatty acid synthesis (Hunkeler et al., 2018; Kleinschmidt et al., 1969), amino acid synthesis (Cohen et al., 1976; Frey et al., 1975; Miller et al., 1974; Petrovska et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2018), and nucleotide synthesis (Barry et al., 2014; Carcamo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on amino acid synthesis enzyme assemblies.

claim: Metabolic enzyme assemblies have been found in nucleotide synthesis.
source: These assemblies have been found in many core pathways including glycolysis (Kemp, 1971; Webb et al., 2017), fatty acid synthesis (Hunkeler et al., 2018; Kleinschmidt et al., 1969), amino acid synthesis (Cohen et al., 1976; Frey et al., 1975; Miller et al., 1974; Petrovska et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2018), and nucleotide synthesis (Barry et al., 2014; Carcamo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on nucleotide synthesis enzyme assemblies.

claim: Metabolic enzymes that form filaments are frequently found at rate-limiting and energetically committed steps of pathways.
source: Metabolic enzymes that form filaments are frequently found at rate-limiting and energetically committed steps of pathways, suggesting filaments play a role in regulating metabolic flux (Noree et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Noree et al., 2019.

claim: For most enzyme polymers that have been functionally characterized, assembly functions as a mechanism of allosteric regulation to tune enzyme activity.
source: Indeed, for most enzyme polymers that have been functionally characterized, assembly functions as a mechanism of allosteric regulation to tune enzyme activity (Barry et al., 2014; Hunkeler et al., 2018; Johnson and Kollman, 2020; Lynch et al., 2017; Lynch and Kollman, 2020; Stoddard et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to functional studies.

claim: CTPS catalyzes the final, rate-limiting step of de novo CTP biosynthesis.
source: CTP synthase (CTPS) catalyzes the final, rate-limiting step of de novo CTP biosynthesis (Lieberman, 1956; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Each CTPS monomer consists of a glutaminase domain and an amido-ligase domain connected by an alpha helical linker.
source: Each CTPS monomer consists of a glutaminase domain and an amido-ligase domain connected by an alpha helical linker (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Glutamine hydrolysis in the glutaminase domain produces ammonia which is transferred through a channel into the amido-ligase domain.
source: Glutamine hydrolysis in the glutaminase domain produces ammonia which is transferred through a channel into the amido-ligase domain, where it is ligated to UTP to form CTP in an ATP-dependent process (Endrizzi et al., 2005; Goto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Ammonia is ligated to UTP to form CTP in an ATP-dependent process in the amido-ligase domain.
source: Glutamine hydrolysis in the glutaminase domain produces ammonia which is transferred through a channel into the amido-ligase domain, where it is ligated to UTP to form CTP in an ATP-dependent process (Endrizzi et al., 2005; Goto et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Substrate binding induces rotation of the glutaminase domain which opens an ammonia channel between active sites.
source: Substrate binding induces rotation of the glutaminase domain which opens an ammonia channel between active sites (Lynch and Kollman, 2020), and it's reaction product CTP inhibits activity (Habrian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: CTP inhibits CTPS activity.
source: Substrate binding induces rotation of the glutaminase domain which opens an ammonia channel between active sites (Lynch and Kollman, 2020), and it's reaction product CTP inhibits activity (Habrian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Habrian et al., 2016.

claim: CTPS assembles X-shaped, D2 symmetric homotetramers through interactions of the amido-ligase domains.
source: CTPS assembles X-shaped, D2 symmetric homotetramers through interactions of the amido-ligase domains, with multiple protomers participating in each substrate and regulatory binding site (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Multiple CTPS protomers participate in each substrate and regulatory binding site.
source: CTPS assembles X-shaped, D2 symmetric homotetramers through interactions of the amido-ligase domains, with multiple protomers participating in each substrate and regulatory binding site (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1c and supported by structural data.

claim: Cellular CTPS filament assembly is widespread across the domains of life, having been observed in bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes.
source: Cellular CTPS filament assembly is widespread across the domains of life, having been observed in bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes (Carcamo et al., 2011; Ingerson-Mahar et al., 2010; Liu, 2010; Noree et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies in different organisms.

claim: There are striking differences between the assembly mechanisms and filament architectures among CTPS from different species.
source: We have previously shown, however, that there are striking differences between the assembly mechanisms and filament architectures among species (Figure 1d–f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1d-f comparing bacterial, human, and yeast CTPS.

claim: Bacterial CTPS filaments provide a mechanism to allosterically inhibit the enzyme.
source: These differences give rise to differences in function, with bacterial CTPS filaments providing a mechanism to allosterically inhibit the enzyme, while animal CTPS filaments act to increase activity and cooperativity of regulation (Barry et al., 2014; Lynch et al., 2017; Lynch and Kollman, 2020; Zhou et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: Animal CTPS filaments act to increase activity and cooperativity of regulation.
source: These differences give rise to differences in function, with bacterial CTPS filaments providing a mechanism to allosterically inhibit the enzyme, while animal CTPS filaments act to increase activity and cooperativity of regulation (Barry et al., 2014; Lynch et al., 2017; Lynch and Kollman, 2020; Zhou et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior functional studies.

claim: During starvation, yeast assemble many metabolic enzymes into filaments.
source: During starvation, yeast assemble many metabolic enzymes into filaments (Narayanaswamy et al., 2009; Noree et al., 2010; Shen et al., 2016) which protects cells and permits rapid growth upon readdition of nutrients (Petrovska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Metabolic enzyme filaments in yeast protect cells and permit rapid growth upon readdition of nutrients.
source: During starvation, yeast assemble many metabolic enzymes into filaments (Narayanaswamy et al., 2009; Noree et al., 2010; Shen et al., 2016) which protects cells and permits rapid growth upon readdition of nutrients (Petrovska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Petrovska et al., 2014.

claim: Polymerization of metabolic enzymes leads to increased cytoplasmic viscosity, limiting diffusion of metabolites and slowing growth.
source: It is thought that polymerization leads to increased cytoplasmic viscosity, limiting diffusion of metabolites and slowing growth (Petrovska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Without energy, membrane-bound proton pumps fail and the neutral-pH cytoplasm is acidified in yeast.
source: Without energy, membrane-bound proton pumps fail and the neutral-pH cytoplasm is acidified (Orij et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Orij et al., 2009.

claim: Acidification is necessary and sufficient for yeast to trigger metabolic filament assembly and effectively mount a stress response.
source: This acidification is necessary and sufficient for yeast to trigger metabolic filament assembly and effectively mount a stress response (Petrovska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Petrovska et al., 2014.

claim: Fluorescence-based studies of tagged CTPS in yeast and other organisms demonstrated large foci or rods consistent with laterally associating filaments.
source: Fluorescence-based studies of tagged CTPS in yeast and other organisms demonstrated large foci or rods consistent with laterally associating filaments (Ingerson-Mahar et al., 2010; Liu, 2010), yet there are no high-resolution structures of bundled metabolic enzymes in any organism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior fluorescence microscopy studies.

claim: There are no high-resolution structures of bundled metabolic enzymes in any organism prior to this study.
source: Fluorescence-based studies of tagged CTPS in yeast and other organisms demonstrated large foci or rods consistent with laterally associating filaments (Ingerson-Mahar et al., 2010; Liu, 2010), yet there are no high-resolution structures of bundled metabolic enzymes in any organism.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: Budding yeast have two CTPS isoforms, Ura7 and Ura8.
source: Budding yeast have two CTPS isoforms, Ura7 (Yang et al., 1994) and Ura8 (Nadkarni et al., 1995; Ozier-Kalogeropoulos et al., 1994), which share 78 % identical residues.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Ura7 and Ura8 share 78% identical residues.
source: Budding yeast have two CTPS isoforms, Ura7 (Yang et al., 1994) and Ura8 (Nadkarni et al., 1995; Ozier-Kalogeropoulos et al., 1994), which share 78 % identical residues.
evidence: This is a sequence comparison result.

claim: Ura7 mRNA is twofold more abundant than Ura8 in vivo.
source: While Ura7 mRNA is twofold more abundant than Ura8 in vivo (Nadkarni et al., 1995), they are functionally overlapping and deletion of either gene results in slowed growth (Ozier-Kalogeropoulos et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nadkarni et al., 1995.

claim: Ura7 and Ura8 are functionally overlapping.
source: While Ura7 mRNA is twofold more abundant than Ura8 in vivo (Nadkarni et al., 1995), they are functionally overlapping and deletion of either gene results in slowed growth (Ozier-Kalogeropoulos et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ozier-Kalogeropoulos et al., 1994.

claim: Deletion of either Ura7 or Ura8 gene results in slowed growth.
source: While Ura7 mRNA is twofold more abundant than Ura8 in vivo (Nadkarni et al., 1995), they are functionally overlapping and deletion of either gene results in slowed growth (Ozier-Kalogeropoulos et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ozier-Kalogeropoulos et al., 1994.

claim: Both Ura7 and Ura8 form supramolecular structures in response to stress that colocalize in cells.
source: Both form supramolecular structures in response to stress that colocalize in cells (Noree et al., 2010; Shen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Ura7-GFP tagged at the endogenous locus forms foci upon nutrient deprivation.
source: Ura7-GFP tagged at the endogenous locus forms foci upon nutrient deprivation (Figure 2a), or when cells are permeabilized with DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol) to manipulate cytoplasmic pH (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Ura7-GFP forms foci when cells are permeabilized with DNP to manipulate cytoplasmic pH.
source: Ura7-GFP tagged at the endogenous locus forms foci upon nutrient deprivation (Figure 2a), or when cells are permeabilized with DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol) to manipulate cytoplasmic pH (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b.

claim: At pH 7.4 both Ura7 and Ura8 assembled short, single filaments on binding substrates or product.
source: At pH 7.4 both isoforms assembled short, single filaments on binding substrates or product, but pH 6.0 promoted assembly of much larger polymers that appeared to be bundled filaments (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by negative stain EM in Figure 2c.

claim: pH 6.0 promoted assembly of much larger polymers that appeared to be bundled filaments for both Ura7 and Ura8.
source: At pH 7.4 both isoforms assembled short, single filaments on binding substrates or product, but pH 6.0 promoted assembly of much larger polymers that appeared to be bundled filaments (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by negative stain EM in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Yeast CTPS assembly is dependent on ligand binding.
source: Thus, like other species (Barry et al., 2014; Lynch et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2019), yeast CTPS assembly is dependent on ligand binding, and the pH sensitivity is intrinsic to the enzyme itself.
evidence: This is demonstrated by negative stain EM showing no assembly in apo state.

claim: The pH sensitivity of yeast CTPS assembly is intrinsic to the enzyme itself.
source: Thus, like other species (Barry et al., 2014; Lynch et al., 2017; Zhou et al., 2019), yeast CTPS assembly is dependent on ligand binding, and the pH sensitivity is intrinsic to the enzyme itself.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro assembly of purified protein at different pHs.

claim: Human CTPS2 polymerizes equally robustly at pH 6.0 and 8.0.
source: We observed equally robust polymerization of purified human CTPS2 (hCTPS2) at pH 6.0 and 8.0, and negative stain EM averages show that filaments formed at different pHs have similar architectures, suggesting that there is no direct effect of pH on hCTPS2 assembly or structure (Figure 2d, inserts).
evidence: This is shown by negative stain EM in Figure 2d.

claim: Human CTPS2 filaments formed at different pHs have similar architectures.
source: We observed equally robust polymerization of purified human CTPS2 (hCTPS2) at pH 6.0 and 8.0, and negative stain EM averages show that filaments formed at different pHs have similar architectures, suggesting that there is no direct effect of pH on hCTPS2 assembly or structure (Figure 2d, inserts).
evidence: This is shown by negative stain EM 2D averages in Figure 2d.

claim: pH-driven assembly of CTPS appears to be specific to yeast.
source: Thus, pH-driven assembly of CTPS appears to be specific to yeast, raising the question of what unique structural features might confer pH-sensitivity.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of yeast and human CTPS assembly at different pHs.

claim: At pH 6, Ura8 assembly was much faster than Ura7.
source: At pH 6, Ura8 assembly was much faster than Ura7, but inspection at early time points showed that both exhibited biphasic assembly which could not be fit with a single equation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by light scattering data in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both Ura7 and Ura8 exhibited biphasic assembly at pH 6.
source: At pH 6, Ura8 assembly was much faster than Ura7, but inspection at early time points showed that both exhibited biphasic assembly which could not be fit with a single equation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by light scattering data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Single filaments appear at early time points and thicker bundles at later time points for Ura7.
source: We examined the growth of Ura7 filaments by negative stain EM over time, and found that single filaments appear at early time points and the thicker bundles at later time points, suggesting that the biphasic scattering kinetics can be explained by initial linear polymerization followed by lateral aggregation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by time-course negative stain EM in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The biphasic scattering kinetics can be explained by initial linear polymerization followed by lateral aggregation.
source: We examined the growth of Ura7 filaments by negative stain EM over time, and found that single filaments appear at early time points and the thicker bundles at later time points, suggesting that the biphasic scattering kinetics can be explained by initial linear polymerization followed by lateral aggregation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the time-course EM data.

claim: Ura8 yielded the highest resolution structures at 2.8 Å (substrates) and 3.8 Å (products).
source: Ura8 yielded the highest resolution structures, at 2.8 Å (substrates) and 3.8 Å (products) (Figure 3a, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 1.

claim: In the Ura8 structures, all ligands were clearly visible and bound as previously described for other CTPS homologs.
source: In the Ura8 structures, all ligands were clearly visible and bound as previously described for other CTPS homologs, including an imino-phosphate reaction intermediate recently observed in Drosophila CTPS, and the presence of two distinct CTP-binding sites per monomer recently reported in human and Drosophila CTPS (Endrizzi et al., 2004; Goto et al., 2004; Lynch et al., 2021; Lynch et al., 2017; Lynch and Kollman, 2020; Zhou et al., 2021; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claim: Ura7 filaments reached lower resolutions, 7.3 Å (substrates) and 3.7 Å (products).
source: Ura7 filaments reached lower resolutions, 7.3 Å (substrates) and 3.7 Å (products), but the overall structures were indistinguishable from Ura8 at these resolutions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Table 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 1.

claim: The overall structures of Ura7 filaments were indistinguishable from Ura8 at these resolutions.
source: Ura7 filaments reached lower resolutions, 7.3 Å (substrates) and 3.7 Å (products), but the overall structures were indistinguishable from Ura8 at these resolutions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Table 2).
evidence: This is shown by comparison in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Yeast CTPS assembles as stacked tetramers using a completely different interaction interface than other species.
source: Like other previously reported structures of human, Drosophila, and E. coli CTPS, the yeast enzyme assembles as stacked tetramers. However, it does so using a completely different interaction interface, which was the same in both substrate- and product-bound yeast structures (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3b and by comparison with other structures.

claim: Helix 356–370 in the glutaminase domain mediates interactions between tetramers in yeast CTPS.
source: Helix 356–370 in the glutaminase domain mediates interactions between tetramers, so that each protomer is involved in assembly contacts (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3b.

claim: His360 interacts with D370 which would be stabilized by protonation of His360 at low pH.
source: His360 interacts with D370 which would be stabilized by protonation of His360 at low pH, and likely explains the pH-sensitivity of the assembly interaction (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The His360-D370 interaction likely explains the pH-sensitivity of the assembly interaction.
source: His360 interacts with D370 which would be stabilized by protonation of His360 at low pH, and likely explains the pH-sensitivity of the assembly interaction (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and chemical properties of histidine.

claim: Helix 356–370 also forms the assembly interface of animal CTPS filaments, but the yeast interface is shifted by two turns of the helix.
source: Helix 356–370 also forms the assembly interface of animal CTPS filaments, but the yeast interface is shifted by two turns of the helix, resulting in completely different residue contacts (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is shown by comparison in Figure 3c.

claim: The yeast CTPS filament interface has a larger buried surface area (706 Å2 per monomer in product-bound filaments) than the human homolog (492 Å2 per monomer in product-bound filaments).
source: This leads to a larger interaction interface in yeast CTPS filaments (706 Å2 per monomer in product-bound filaments) than in the human homolog (492 Å2 per monomer in product-bound filaments) (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is calculated from the structures and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The Ura8 product-bound filament is in the canonical inhibited conformation.
source: The Ura8 product-bound filament is in the canonical inhibited conformation, but the substrate-bound structure is in a conformation intermediate between canonical active and inhibited states, in which the ammonia channel remains closed.
evidence: This is determined from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The substrate-bound Ura8 filament structure is in a conformation intermediate between canonical active and inhibited states, in which the ammonia channel remains closed.
source: The Ura8 product-bound filament is in the canonical inhibited conformation, but the substrate-bound structure is in a conformation intermediate between canonical active and inhibited states, in which the ammonia channel remains closed.
evidence: This is determined from the cryo-EM structure and shown in Figure 3f.

claim: In the unassembled state at pH 7.4, Ura8 adopts the canonical active conformation, very similar to hCTPS2.
source: In this unassembled state, Ura8 adopts the canonical active conformation, very similar to hCTPS2, including opening of the ammonia channel and rearrangement at the tetramerization interface (Figure 3d–h, Figure 3—figure supplement 5, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is shown by the cryo-EM structure of free tetramers in Figure 3d-h.

claim: The active state observed in free tetramers is incompatible with filament assembly.
source: The active state we observe in free tetramers is incompatible with filament assembly, because in this conformation filament interfaces cannot be occupied on both sides of the tetramer simultaneously (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is shown by modeling in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Filament assembly with symmetric contacts acts as a steric constraint to trap yeast CTPS in a low activity conformation.
source: Thus, filament assembly with symmetric contacts acts as a steric constraint to trap yeast CTPS in a low activity conformation, while tethering through a single glutaminase domain supports short, flexible filaments that accommodate a fully active conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and modeling.

claim: Ura7-H360A did not assembly filaments with substrates or products at low or high pH.
source: Consistent with those prior results, Ura7-H360A did not assembly filaments with substrates or products at low or high pH (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is shown by negative stain EM in Figure 4a.

claim: Ura7-H360R robustly assembles filaments at pH 7.4.
source: Indeed, we found that Ura7-H360R robustly assembles filaments at pH 7.4 which, like the wild-type protein, assemble only in the presence of substrate or product ligands (Figure 4a, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by negative stain EM in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reversible assembly of H360R into wildtype-like filaments is pH-insensitive.
source: Thus, reversible assembly of H360R into wiltype-like filaments is pH-insensitive.
evidence: This is demonstrated by assembly at pH 7.4 shown in Figure 4a.

claim: H360A had approximately threefold higher activity than wildtype at pH 6.0.
source: Consistent with this, Ura7 wildtype, H360A, and H360R all have low activity at pH 6.0. However, H360A had approximately threefold higher activity, indicating that unassembled CTPS maintains residual activity even at low pH (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is shown by activity assays in Figure 4b.

claim: Unassembled CTPS maintains residual activity even at low pH.
source: Consistent with this, Ura7 wildtype, H360A, and H360R all have low activity at pH 6.0. However, H360A had approximately threefold higher activity, indicating that unassembled CTPS maintains residual activity even at low pH (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is inferred from the H360A activity data at pH 6.0.

claim: The KM values were similar for wildtype Ura7 and both mutants.
source: The KM values were similar for wildtype and both mutants, indicating no change in affinity for the substrate UTP.
evidence: This is shown by substrate kinetics in Figure 4c and Table 3.

claim: Vmax varied inversely with the degree of filament assembly for Ura7 wildtype and mutants.
source: However, Vmax varied inversely with the degree of filament assembly (Figure 4c, Table 3).
evidence: This is shown by substrate kinetics in Figure 4c and Table 3.

claim: At pH 7.4 Ura7-H360A is completely tetrameric and had the highest activity.
source: At pH 7.4 Ura7-H360A is completely tetrameric and had the highest activity, wild-type enzyme has a background of single filaments and had slightly lower activity, and Ura7-H360R had robust filament assembly and the lowest observed activity.
evidence: This is shown by activity assays in Figure 4c.

claim: Wild-type Ura7 has a background of single filaments at pH 7.4 and had slightly lower activity than H360A.
source: At pH 7.4 Ura7-H360A is completely tetrameric and had the highest activity, wild-type enzyme has a background of single filaments and had slightly lower activity, and Ura7-H360R had robust filament assembly and the lowest observed activity.
evidence: This is shown by activity assays in Figure 4c and negative stain EM.

claim: Ura7-H360R had robust filament assembly and the lowest observed activity at pH 7.4.
source: At pH 7.4 Ura7-H360A is completely tetrameric and had the highest activity, wild-type enzyme has a background of single filaments and had slightly lower activity, and Ura7-H360R had robust filament assembly and the lowest observed activity.
evidence: This is shown by activity assays in Figure 4c and negative stain EM.

claim: Filament assembly in itself acts as an allosteric inhibitor of enzyme activity.
source: This suggests that filament assembly in itself acts as an allosteric inhibitor of enzyme activity, with kcat reduced likely as a consequence of the constricted ammonia channel we observe in the filament structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between assembly and activity.

claim: Cells expressing non-assembling Ura7-H360A-GFP or Ura8-H360A-GFP did not form foci, even under nutritional stress.
source: Consistent with our in vitro findings, cells expressing non-assembling Ura7-H360A-GFP or Ura8-H360A-GFP did not form foci, even under nutritional stress when the cytoplasm is acidified (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is shown by fluorescence microscopy in Figure 5a.

claim: The non-assembly single mutants of Ura7 or Ura8 grew indistinguishably from wild type during log phase and upon recovery from starvation.
source: The non-assembly single mutants of Ura7 or Ura8 grew indistinguishably from wild type during log phase and upon recovery from starvation (Figure 5d–e, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by growth assays in Figure 5d-e.

claim: The double mutant URA7-H360A/URA8-H360A had a severe growth defect in log phase and upon starvation recovery.
source: To test this, we generated the double mutant URA7-H360A/URA8-H360A, and found that it had a severe growth defect in log phase and upon starvation recovery (Figure 5d–e), indicating an important role for CTPS polymerization in proliferation.
evidence: This is shown by growth assays in Figure 5d-e.

claim: CTPS polymerization plays an important role in proliferation.
source: To test this, we generated the double mutant URA7-H360A/URA8-H360A, and found that it had a severe growth defect in log phase and upon starvation recovery (Figure 5d–e), indicating an important role for CTPS polymerization in proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth defect of the double mutant.

claim: Wildtype Ura7 levels are decreased during starvation.
source: Wildtype Ura7 levels are decreased during starvation, but there was no difference in protein levels between wild type and the mutants at 4 or 24 hr of starvation (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: There was no difference in Ura7 protein levels between wild type and the mutants at 4 or 24 hr of starvation.
source: Wildtype Ura7 levels are decreased during starvation, but there was no difference in protein levels between wild type and the mutants at 4 or 24 hr of starvation (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Filament assembly does not play a significant role in protecting CTPS from degradation.
source: This indicates that filament assembly does not play a significant role in protecting CTPS from degradation, and suggests that growth defects observed upon starvation recovery for URA7-H360A/URA8-H360A arise from other effects of defective polymerization.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data showing similar protein levels.

claim: Ura7-H360R grew more slowly than wildtype when plated either from log phase cultures or from starved cultures.
source: In addition to disrupted assembly kinetics, Ura7-H360R grew more slowly than wildtype, when plated either from log phase cultures or from starved cultures (Figure 5d–e), suggesting that disruption of normal Ura7 assembly and disassembly is generally detrimental to growth.
evidence: This is shown by growth assays in Figure 5d-e.

claim: Disruption of normal Ura7 assembly and disassembly is generally detrimental to growth.
source: In addition to disrupted assembly kinetics, Ura7-H360R grew more slowly than wildtype, when plated either from log phase cultures or from starved cultures (Figure 5d–e), suggesting that disruption of normal Ura7 assembly and disassembly is generally detrimental to growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth defect of H360R mutant.

claim: Ura7-H360R-GFP assembly and disassembly kinetics are dysregulated.
source: However, Ura7-H360R-GFP assembly and disassembly kinetics are dysregulated (Figure 5b–c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—videos 1–4).
evidence: This is shown by live cell imaging in Figure 5b-c.

claim: Upon transition to starvation media, wildtype Ura7-GFP typically assembles foci over the course of 30 min.
source: Upon transition to starvation media, wildtype Ura7-GFP typically assembles foci over the course of 30 min, but Ura7-H360R-GFP assembles more rapidly, with virtually all cells having foci at 5 min.
evidence: This is shown by live cell imaging in Figure 5b.

claim: Ura7-H360R-GFP assembles more rapidly than wildtype, with virtually all cells having foci at 5 min after starvation.
source: Upon transition to starvation media, wildtype Ura7-GFP typically assembles foci over the course of 30 min, but Ura7-H360R-GFP assembles more rapidly, with virtually all cells having foci at 5 min.
evidence: This is shown by live cell imaging in Figure 5b.

claim: Upon recovery from starvation, wild-type Ura7 disassembles in most cells after 30 min.
source: Even more striking, upon recovery from starvation, in which wild-type Ura7 disassembles in most cells after 30 min, at 1 hr we did not observe significant depolymerization of Ura7-H360R-GFP foci (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by live cell imaging in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 1 hr after recovery from starvation, there was no significant depolymerization of Ura7-H360R-GFP foci.
source: Even more striking, upon recovery from starvation, in which wild-type Ura7 disassembles in most cells after 30 min, at 1 hr we did not observe significant depolymerization of Ura7-H360R-GFP foci (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by live cell imaging in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The starvation-triggered pH change is necessary but not sufficient to enable cellular Ura7 assembly.
source: The rapid assembly and slow disassembly of Ura7-H360R in cells are consistent with the in vitro pH-insensitive phenotype, but suggest that the starvation-triggered pH change is necessary but not sufficient to enable cellular Ura7 assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that H360R does not assemble during log phase despite being pH-insensitive in vitro.

claim: Ura8 bundle structures were determined at 3.3 Å for substrates and 3.7 Å for product.
source: As we found for the single filament structures, Ura8 reconstructions went to higher resolution (3.3 Å for substrates and 3.7 Å for product) than Ura7 (6.6 Å substrate and 7.0 Å product).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 1.

claim: Ura7 bundle structures were determined at 6.6 Å substrate and 7.0 Å product.
source: As we found for the single filament structures, Ura8 reconstructions went to higher resolution (3.3 Å for substrates and 3.7 Å for product) than Ura7 (6.6 Å substrate and 7.0 Å product).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 1.

claim: Ura7 formed very similar bundles in both ligand conditions, with adjacent filaments staggered relative to each other with a half-tetramer offset.
source: Ura7 formed very similar bundles in both ligand conditions, with adjacent filaments staggered relative to each other with a half-tetramer offset (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is shown by cryo-EM structures in Figure 6.

claim: The Ura8 substrate-bound structure had the same architecture as both Ura7 bundles.
source: The Ura8 substrate-bound structure had the same architecture as both Ura7 bundles, but the product-bound Ura8 structure had very different interfaces between filaments, giving rise to filaments in register (Figure 6d, Figure 6—videos 1–4).
evidence: This is shown by cryo-EM structures in Figure 6.

claim: The product-bound Ura8 structure had very different interfaces between filaments, giving rise to filaments in register.
source: The Ura8 substrate-bound structure had the same architecture as both Ura7 bundles, but the product-bound Ura8 structure had very different interfaces between filaments, giving rise to filaments in register (Figure 6d, Figure 6—videos 1–4).
evidence: This is shown by cryo-EM structures in Figure 6d.

claim: The buried surface area per tetramer at lateral interfaces is 2202 Å2 (substrates-bound) or 1676 Å2 (product-bound).
source: The buried surface area per tetramer at lateral interfaces, 2202 Å2 (substrates-bound) or 1676 Å2 (product-bound), is comparable to the 2460 Å2 involved in longitudinal filament assembly contacts, suggesting that lateral association contributes to the overall stability of the assembly (Figure 6—figure supplement 4, Table 4).
evidence: This is calculated from the structures and shown in Table 4.

claim: Yeast CTPS has a 7-residue insert (residues 273–279) in the linker region that mediates the bulk of the lateral interaction in both bundle types.
source: Yeast CTPS has a 7-residue insert (residues 273–279) in the linker region that mediates the bulk of the lateral interaction in both bundle types (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is shown by structural analysis in Figure 6e-g.

claim: In the substrate-bound structure, Leu277 nestles into a hydrophobic pocket formed by Ile383/Ile387/Ile412/Phe429.
source: In the substrate-bound structure, Leu277 nestles into a hydrophobic pocket formed by Ile383/Ile387/Ile412/Phe429 (Figure 6f, Figure 6—figure supplement 5a,b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6f and Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Similar filament bundles have not been reported for other species, despite extensive structural characterization of human, Drosophila, and E. coli CTPS filaments.
source: Similar filament bundles have not been reported for other species, despite extensive structural characterization of human, Drosophila, and E. coli CTPS filaments (Barry et al., 2014; Lynch et al., 2017; Lynch and Kollman, 2020; Zhou et al., 2021), suggesting that the unique yeast insert promotes lateral assemblies that are specific to yeast.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published structures.

claim: The unique yeast insert promotes lateral assemblies that are specific to yeast.
source: Similar filament bundles have not been reported for other species, despite extensive structural characterization of human, Drosophila, and E. coli CTPS filaments (Barry et al., 2014; Lynch et al., 2017; Lynch and Kollman, 2020; Zhou et al., 2021), suggesting that the unique yeast insert promotes lateral assemblies that are specific to yeast.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data and comparison with other species.

claim: Budding yeast CTPS assembles filaments with a distinct assembly interface that maintains the enzyme in a low activity state.
source: We have shown that budding yeast CTPS assembles filaments with yet another, distinct assembly interface that maintains the enzyme in a low activity state.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural and activity data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The diversity of CTPS filament structure and function raises the question of whether this reflects modification of an ancestral filament structure, or whether CTPS polymerization has evolved independently multiple times.
source: The diversity of CTPS filament structure and function raises the question of whether this reflects modification of an ancestral filament structure, or whether CTPS polymerization has evolved independently multiple times.
evidence: This is a question posed based on the observed diversity.

claim: The yeast CTPS filament has acquired features that make its assembly responsive to cytoplasmic changes in nutrient availability and growth conditions.
source: Whatever its evolutionary origins, the yeast CTPS filament has acquired features that make its assembly responsive to cytoplasmic changes in nutrient availability and growth conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the pH-sensitive assembly mechanism.

claim: Yeast CTPS polymerization is a self-assembly mechanism that does not require other cellular factors.
source: We have shown here that yeast CTPS polymerization is a self-assembly mechanism that does not require other cellular factors, and that the pH-sensitivity of CTPS polymers is intrinsic to the enzyme itself (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro assembly of purified protein.

claim: In the filament, CTPS is held in a conformation that closes off an internal ammonia channel that likely reduces activity.
source: In the filament, CTPS is held in a conformation that closes off an internal ammonia channel that likely reduces activity (Figure 3f and h).
evidence: This is shown by structural analysis in Figure 3f and h.

claim: Assembly is correlated with reduced activity at neutral pH and at low pH.
source: Mutations at the assembly interface that either block assembly (H360A) or eliminate the pH sensitivity (H360R) showed that assembly is correlated with reduced activity, both at neutral pH where the wildtype enzyme forms short single polymers, and at low pH where the wild-type enzyme forms large laterally assembled bundles that are threefold less active than the non-assembling mutant (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is shown by activity assays in Figure 4b-c.

claim: Yeast has a strong propensity to assemble CTPS laterally that is intrinsic to the purified protein.
source: Yeast, on the other hand, has a strong propensity to assemble laterally that is intrinsic to the purified protein, driven by a yeast-specific insert in the linker domain that mediates well-ordered lateral contacts.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro assembly and structural analysis.

claim: The low residual activity of tetrameric CTPS at low pH may be sufficient to imbalance nucleotide pools over prolonged starvation.
source: One possibility may be that the low residual activity of tetrameric CTPS at low pH is sufficient to imbalance nucleotide pools over prolonged starvation.
evidence: This is speculation about the function of pH-sensitive assembly.

claim: Upon reintroduction of glucose the cytoplasm returns to neutral pH over about 2 min.
source: Upon reintroduction of glucose the cytoplasm returns to neutral pH over about 2 min (Orij et al., 2009), but CTPS filaments disassemble over about 30 min or longer (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which may enable a more controlled ramping up of enzyme activity upon re-entering growth.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Orij et al., 2009.

claim: CTPS filaments disassemble over about 30 min or longer upon recovery from starvation.
source: Upon reintroduction of glucose the cytoplasm returns to neutral pH over about 2 min (Orij et al., 2009), but CTPS filaments disassemble over about 30 min or longer (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which may enable a more controlled ramping up of enzyme activity upon re-entering growth.
evidence: This is shown by live cell imaging in Figure 5c.

claim: Disruption of CTPS polymerization likely results in disruption of nucleotide homeostasis.
source: Disruption of polymerization-based allosteric regulation of CTPS likely results in disruption of nucleotide homeostasis, with potential consequences for processes that depend on nucleotide pools like ribosome biosynthesis, DNA replication, and phospholipid biosynthesis (Chang and Carman, 2008; Fairbanks et al., 1995).
evidence: This is speculation based on the known role of CTPS and supported by citations.

claim: Disrupting Ura7 in yeast is strongly mutagenic, particularly during the stress response.
source: Further, disruption of CTPS increases genomic instability (Whelan et al., 1993), and specifically disrupting Ura7 in yeast is strongly mutagenic, particularly during the stress response (Schmidt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.
